lectures.title: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP): the Dynamics of IP Packet Transmission

cues.en: In this lecture, I want to ask the question, How do we know where we need to send a frame to?
Let me give you an example.
So let's say we got our network here, we got a router and we got our network here.
You can see here I've added the Mac addresses here because I will need this to explain something.
Let's say we are this computer and we want to send an IP packet to this IP.
So we create the packet.
We say, okay, this is the IP that we want to send it to, but if we want to send an IP packet, we
need to take, okay, here we have data from our IP packet.
Then we add a so-called IP packet header.
That's why it's here on top.
This header will contain various fields.
So for example, this is our IP, but the most important one is this is the two IP or the destination
IP.
We want to send this packet from this computer to this computer.
So we got the data that we want to transfer and we got our IP headers telling, Hey, this is the IP
that this package should reach.
But if we want to send it through our network, we need to put it onto an Ethernet frame.
So we need to know the Mac address of the other computer because we need to on the Ethernet layer,
on the layer below, we need to address this Ethernet frame by the Mac address to be able to send it
to here or even if we want to send an IP packet to the internet, we might have an IP address here that's
in the internet.

that's meant for the internet, we put it onto an Ethernet frame that's address to our router and then
the router will just forward this packet, put it on a new frame, send it to the internet and so on.
So the question is, if we want to say, for example, ping this computer, how does it know which Mac
address it should reach on an Ethernet layer?
